A skill is the ability to do something well — an ability that you have developed through learning, practice, and experience.

The two most important parts of that definition are "do something well" and "developed." A skill is not just vague potential. It is a real, working ability that you can actually use. And it doesn't come to you naturally at birth — you build it over time.

Examples: cooking, driving, public speaking, writing code, playing chess, negotiating a deal, reading a map — these are all skills.

A skill has three defining characteristics:

1. It is practical.
A skill is always about doing — performing an action, producing a result, handling a situation. Pure knowing is not a skill. You can read twenty books about swimming and know exactly how the arms and legs should move — but that knowledge alone is not a skill. The skill is swimming itself, the ability to actually get in the water and do it.

2. It is learned and developed.
This is what sets a skill apart from a raw, inborn trait. Nobody is born already knowing how to code or negotiate. You acquire a skill through deliberate effort: instruction, repetition, correction, and experience. This also means skills can be taught, improved, and lost if unused.

3. It involves a level of competence — doing it well.
Not every attempt at something counts as having the skill. If someone has never driven a car before and manages to move it three metres, we wouldn't say they have a "driving skill." A skill implies a reliable, reasonably competent ability. The more reliably and expertly you can do something, the stronger your skill in it.

Skills exist on a spectrum from beginner to master.

You might have a basic skill — you can do the thing, but only in straightforward situations and with some effort. Or you might have an advanced skill — you do it quickly, fluently, and in complex situations without much conscious effort.

This is why we talk about someone having "strong" or "weak" skills, being "highly skilled" or "unskilled" at something. Skill is not an on/off switch; it is a measure of how well you can do something.

A person who has taken one cooking class has some cooking skill. A chef who has cooked thousands of dishes over ten years has highly developed cooking skill. The word covers both — but context tells you the degree.

You will often hear skills divided into two broad categories:

Hard skills are technical, specific, and usually measurable. They often relate to a particular job, tool, or domain. Examples: speaking a foreign language, operating machinery, writing software, performing surgery, playing the violin, using accounting software.

Soft skills are interpersonal and behavioural abilities — how you work with others and handle yourself. Examples: communication, leadership, time management, empathy, problem-solving, adaptability.

Both are real skills. The word "soft" doesn't mean less important — in many careers, soft skills are just as valued as technical ones.

The word works naturally in both singular and plural.

  • One skill: "Public speaking is a skill I want to develop." (referring to one specific ability)
  • Multiple skills: "She brought many skills to the team." (a range of abilities)
  • Skills as a collective: "His skills in carpentry are impressive." (here, "skills" refers to the full set of abilities he has within a domain)

When we say someone has "skill" (without an article, uncountable), we mean general competence or mastery — a more abstract quality. "She performed the surgery with great skill." This is about the quality of expertise itself, not listing individual abilities.

When we say someone has "a skill" or "skills" (countable), we're pointing to specific, nameable abilities. "He has a rare skill: the ability to stay calm under pressure."

Both uses are common and correct.

Knowing how "skill" combines with other words will help you use and recognise it naturally:

  • Develop a skill — to build an ability over time through practice
  • Acquire a skill — to gain a new ability (often through training)
  • Hone a skill — to refine and sharpen an already existing ability
  • Master a skill — to reach a very high level of ability
  • Apply a skill — to use an ability in a real situation
  • Transferable skills — abilities learned in one context that are useful in another (e.g., communication skills learned in teaching can be used in business)
  • Skill set — the complete collection of skills a person has
  • Skill gap — when the skills someone has don't match what a job or task requires
  • Core skills / key skills — the most essential abilities in a particular field
  • Life skills — practical abilities needed for everyday adult life (budgeting, cooking, navigating conflict)
Skill vs. Words That Feel Similar

Skill vs. Talent:
Talent suggests a natural, inborn gift — something you were born with. Skill is what you build through effort. Someone might have a talent for music (a natural ear, quick learning) but still need to develop skill (years of practice, technique) to perform well. In everyday speech, people sometimes use the words loosely, but strictly speaking, talent is innate and skill is earned.

Skill vs. Ability:
Ability is broader — it refers to any capacity you have, whether natural or learned. Skill is more specific: it always implies something learned and implies a certain standard of performance. All skills are abilities, but not all abilities are skills. Having good eyesight is an ability, not a skill. Being a skilled archer, though, is a skill.

Skill vs. Knowledge:
Knowledge is what you know in your mind. Skill is what you can do. You need some knowledge to build a skill, but knowledge alone is not enough. The difference: a doctor reading a textbook about surgery gains knowledge; a doctor who has performed hundreds of operations has skill.

Skill vs. Experience:
Experience is time spent doing something. Skill is what you've actually built as a result. Ten years of experience doesn't automatically mean ten years of skill growth — it depends on whether you were learning and improving. Experience and skill often go together, but they aren't the same thing.

"Skill" is one of the most practically important words in any language because it names something central to human achievement. It captures the idea that most valuable human capabilities are not accidents of birth — they are built. That framing carries a quiet but powerful implication: almost any skill, with enough time and the right effort, can be developed by almost anyone.

When you understand the word deeply, you see it used this way constantly — in education, hiring, sports, art, medicine, and everyday conversation — always pointing to that same core idea: a real, developed ability to do something well.
